newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Crew set to return to Earth after six-month ordeal.
newsitem.headline: Crew set to return to Earth after six-month ordeal.

text.p: Two Russian cosmonauts aboard Mir made final preparations on Wednesday to return to Earth after one of the most gruelling missions in the space station's 11-year history, officials said.

Russian commander Vasily Tsibliyev and engineer Alexander Lazutkin have endured a series of major woes since they came aboard in February. The most serious incident was a June 25 collision between Mir and its resupply ship.
Mir has run on partial power since then.

After the crash, the worst in Mir's history, Tsibliyev began suffering heart irregularities which doctors said was related to stress. He was given heart medication that has since been discontinued, and will take no special pills for his Thursday return, a top medical adviser said.
"There will be no special medication or measures for his return; everything is routine," Irina Alfyerova, head of Mission Control's medical group, told Reuters.
"He's just taking the usual at the final stage of the flight such as vitamin supplements and mineral-salted water."
Tsibliyev and Lazutkin planned to enter a Soyuz capsule at 9:50 a.m. (0550 GMT) on Thursday, undock at 12:53 (0853 GMT) and land at 4:16 p.m. (1216 GMT) in the former Soviet republic of Kazakhstan.
They will return to the Moscow region that night, and begin a period of rehabilitation at the Star City cosmonaut training centre that typically lasts three to four weeks.

Their replacement Russian cosmonauts, commander Anatoly Solovyov and engineer Pavel Vinogradov, as well as NASA astronaut Michael Foale, also prepared on Wednesday to fly their escape capsule to another docking port on Mir, said Valery Lyndin, a spokesman for Mission Control outside Moscow.
During that 45-minute operation planned for Friday the crew will take photos of the sealed-off Spektr module, which suffered a puncture in the June accident.

The new crew has already had a taste of some of the repair difficulties that lie ahead. Efforts to restart either of two Elektron oxygen generating systems have failed, and frustrated engineers are now devising a method to clean out a blocked system pipe in the newer main Elektron with a mixture of aspirin and water, NASA said.
In the meantime, the crew is relying on a back-up system of oxygen "candles".

Mir's "urine reclamation system", which purifies the station's water, has also been off to save power. Tsibliyev and Lazutkin will bring back samples for experts on Earth to test after they return on Thursday.
NASA said the U.S. space shuttle bringing on about September 27 Foale's replacement, David Wolf, would also be carrying more water.
After Tsibliyev and Lazutkin leave, the remaining crew will intensify preparations for a risky operation planned for August 20 to restore power from the solar panels on Spektr.

Also on Wednesday, Valery Ryumin, a veteran cosmonaut who heads Russia's cooperation with NASA, said the American space agency had asked Moscow to include Foale, a British-American physicist, in a September 3 spacewalk to inspect Spektr, contradicting NASA, which said the request was a Russian idea.

"It wasn't our request, it was the request of the Americans," Ryumin said. "They want to get experience; we responded positively," he told Reuters. "It will probably take place although it has not been decided conclusively."
NASA officials say the first they heard of the idea came when Flight Director Vladimir Solovyov announced Foale's participation at a news conference last week.
